newsitem.title: USA: World Bank sees first debt relief pacts by yearend.
newsitem.headline: World Bank sees first debt relief pacts by yearend.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn said on Friday the international community was near agreement on a debt relief plan for poor nations and expected the first cases to be dealt with by the end of the year.
"My guess is that between now and the end of the year we will have our first cases," Wolfensohn said.

At issue is a joint initiative by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and Paris Club to help countries for whom the benefits of economic growth are eaten up immediately by debt repayments. Many of those nations are in Africa. Uganda is expected to be the first to benefit.
"I think we're very close to reaching a positive and productive agreement that will allow us to proceed immediately on specific cases," Wolfensohn said.

Deputy finance ministers from the Group of Seven rich industrialised nations were trying to settle their differences on Friday over the contribution to be made by the Paris Club of creditor nations to the debt initiative, officials said.

G7 finance ministers -- from the United States, Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Italy and Britain -- are hoping to sketch out some of the details of the Paris Club contribution after their meeting here on Saturday.

The IMF appears to have sidestepped for now a row over whether it should sell a small portion of its gold reserves to finance its share of the initiative by agreeing it has enough money for the time being to contribute.

As regards the World Bank, Wolfensohn said it was willing to put some $2 billion forward for the next few years to contribute to the debt programme, reaffirming a commitment made at a G7 summit in Lyon, France in June.
But details of the Paris Club's plans to improve debt relief have yet to be announced.

The IMF and World Bank had initially called for the Paris Club to forgive some 90 percent of loans, compared to 67 percent currently available for the world's poorest nations, under so-called Naples terms of debt relief.

In reality, Naples terms offer a write-off of much less than that since usually only a part of the debt owed is covered by any Paris Club agreement ahead of a cut-off date often fixed in the early 1980s.
Countries remain obliged to pay debt servicing on loans taken out after that to maintain their creditworthiness.
Wolfensohn said the Paris Club improved debt relief would be less than 90 percent, but he was uncertain by how much.
"I don't know if it's 80 percent but it certainly not going to be 90 percent," he said.

Diplomatic sources said there appeared to be a consensus emerging to offer debt relief of up to 80 percent on a case-by-case basis. Paris Club officials had no comment on the likely scale of its proposed debt relief.
Private development agency Oxfam International slammed the Paris Club for dragging its heels on debt relief.
"Without a clear commitment from the Paris Club to reduce 90 percent of debt, the viability of the entire initiative could be undermined," the group said in a statement.

According to some estimates, about four or five countries would not be able to put their economies back on even keel and achieve so-called debt sustainability if the Paris Club only extends 80 percent debt relief.
